metadata.title: Organizational Capital, Skills and Productivity

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to construct numeracy and task-based ICT/STEM skill indicators, then aggregates them to country–industry level measures. The analysis is conducted at the country–industry level (e.g., 260 observations in preferred regression models), and the paper does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or replicate weights in the econometric estimation. Instead, it applies a custom imputation procedure for missing occupation/skill coverage using country clusters and weighted ratios with a minimum cell-size threshold (20 observations per cell), and it drops industries with insufficient coverage (e.g., agriculture, mining, utilities, real estate). Because the paper does not describe complex survey weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) for the final regressions, weighting is treated as not reported for the econometric stage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not estimate cognitive achievement using PIAAC plausible values (PV) in the sense used for ILSA achievement scales; instead, it constructs numeracy and task-based ICT/STEM indicators and then aggregates them to country–industry level. Missingness is addressed via an occupation/skill-score imputation procedure based on country clusters and weighted ratios, but the paper does not describe this as a standard PV-combining or missing-data imputation method (e.g., multiple imputation) with a clear missing-data handling label. Therefore, missing-data handling is not reported in the schema sense, even though a bespoke imputation approach is used.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PIAAC-based skill indicators (numeracy and task-based ICT/STEM) and constructs OC-related occupation groups; countries are included independently of PIAAC round but are dropped when other datasets are limited or when the OC occupation sample in PIAAC has fewer than 20 observations. For the preferred regression models, the analytic unit is country–industry; industries are dropped when data coverage is insufficient (agriculture ISIC A; mining B; utilities D; water/sewerage/waste management E; real estate L). Additionally, three economies are not considered: Australia (insufficient occupation-level detail at two-digit ISCO08), Cyprus and Russia (small sample sizes). R&D expenditure is lagged by 1 year and is available for 208 of 260 country–industry cells, so models including R&D have fewer observations. Robustness checks are reported in appendices, and standard errors are clustered at the country level.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (Survey of Adult Skills) 2011-2012 (first wave for USA) — numeracy and task-based ICT/STEM indicators aggregated to country–industry level
main_findings.target_variable: Labor productivity (log value added per employee)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS correlations (Table 5, preferred specification model 5): numeracy score coefficient 0.018 (SE 0.008); ICT score ratio coefficient −0.242 (SE 0.112); STEM score (non-OC) coefficient 0.014 (SE 0.005); STEM score ratio (OC/non-OC) coefficient 0.302 (SE 0.128); log net fixed assets/empl. coefficient 0.160 (SE 0.021). Observations: 260; R-squared: 0.917. Three-step Heckman + IV results (Table 6, column 16): STEM (non-OC) coefficient 0.026 (statistically significant); ICT and STEM ratio variables become statistically insignificant; IMR small and statistically insignificant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC (Survey of Adult Skills) data aggregated to country–industry level, the study leveraged numeracy score, ICT ratio (OC/non-OC), STEM score (non-OC), STEM ratio (OC/non-OC), and physical capital intensity to explain labor productivity, finding that numeracy and STEM are positively associated with productivity while a larger ICT skills gap between OC and non-OC workers is negatively correlated with productivity. This indicates that productivity policies should prioritize narrowing ICT skill gaps between organizational-capital (OC) staff and other workers, while also raising STEM skill endowments—though the paper’s IV/selection approach supports robustness rather than definitive causality.

data.outcome_summary: The paper links organizational capital (OC) and workforce skills to industry-level labor productivity using OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) skill indicators (numeracy plus task-based ICT and STEM measures) aggregated to country–industry cells. It includes 21 countries (AUT, BEL, CAN, CZE, DEU, DNK, EST, FIN, FRA, GBR, GRC, HUN, IRL, ITA, LTU, NLD, NOR, POL, SVK, SVN, SWE, and the first wave of USA) and estimates OLS models with country and industry-cluster fixed effects, using 260 observations in the preferred specification (R² ≈ 0.917). The results show that a one-point increase in numeracy is associated with roughly a 1.8–2.4% higher productivity, STEM (non-OC) is positively related to productivity, and the ICT ratio (OC/non-OC) is negatively correlated with productivity (a 0.1 increase corresponds to about 2.34% less productivity). A three-step Heckman selection plus instrumental variables approach yields broadly similar coefficient magnitudes, but the authors caution that exclusion restrictions may be violated, so causal interpretation remains limited. The study also uses a bespoke cluster-based imputation for missing skill coverage and drops industries with insufficient coverage, which may affect comparability across cells.
